results.title: 44% Cheaper H100s: How EU Teams Should Plan GPU Capacity
highlights:
GPU capacity planning changed on June 1, 2025. AWS announced up to a 45 percent price reduction for EC2 NVIDIA GPU-accelerated instances covering the P4 and P5 families, effective on On-Demand purchases and extended to Savings Plans days later. The P5 H100 on-demand rate dropped 44 percent, the deepest on-demand cut in the published table. For engineering teams in Portugal and the wider EU, the reduction cuts both ways: reserved H100-class compute is materially cheaper, and every capacity budget built on the old price list is stale. The demand side is not in question. 13.5 percent of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees used AI technologies in 2024, up from 8.0 percent in 2023, so pressure on accelerated capacity is structural rather than cyclical. This guide covers what the new pricing changes, how reservation mechanics behave, and which calculations EU teams should re-run this quarter.

...

The reduction is a deliberate supply-and-demand lever. AWS framed it against a market where growth in GPU demand has outpaced industry-wide supply, and applied it across every region where the affected families are sold. The published reduction table is uneven, and that unevenness is the useful signal: the newest, most contested silicon got the deepest cut. The H100-backed P5 family received 44 percent off on-demand rates, while the older A100-backed P4 families received 33 percent and the H200-backed P5en received 25 percent. When a hyperscaler discounts its flagship accelerator hardest, it is pricing to keep large training workloads from drifting to neocloud competitors — and that same discount is your negotiating baseline with every other vendor.

| Instance family | Accelerator | On-demand reduction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P4d | A100 | 33% |
| P4de | A100 | 33% |
| P5 | H100 | 44% |
| P5en | H200 | 25% |

results.title: AWS posts new Capacity Block GPU rates effective October 7. · Sayer
results.author: Sayer Staff
highlights:
Amazon Web Services has posted new reservation rates for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, effective October 7, 2026. The prices are hourly, per accelerator: $16.146 for P6-B300 ($16.819 in AWS GovCloud), $14.208 for P6-B200 ($14.801 in GovCloud), $7.895 for P5en, $6.866 for P5e, $5.970 for P5, $2.546 for P4de, and $1.696 for P4d. AWS did not state a percentage.

The company says Capacity Block prices move with supply and demand and are updated from time to time. On its pricing page it says the new rates apply across available regions for those families. It also says every other EC2 Capacity Block price stays the same, and that prices on fixed models such as On-Demand and Savings Plans do not change. UltraServer and Trainium Capacity Block rates are on the current tables and are not in the October 7 list.

A Capacity Block is charged at the rate in effect when the customer buys it, AWS says, even if the block is scheduled to start after a later update. The fee is paid up front.

News outlets, citing Wells Fargo rather than quoting a public research note, have described a reserved-GPU increase of about 15 percent on October 7 and called it a fourth straight quarterly hike. Cointelegraph wrote that AWS is raising reserved GPU prices by 15 percent on Oct. 7, “marking its fourth straight quarterly hike, per Wells Fargo.” Roic AI, attributing the figure to Wells Fargo, said reserved GPU compute prices would rise 15 percent on October 7 after a 20 percent increase in July, and described the step as the fourth consecutive quarterly increase. No Wells Fargo note was available to quote directly, and none of those percentages appears on the AWS page. AWS’s own line is the dollar rates above, not “15 percent.”

The analyst shorthand is also wider than the product AWS named. The public write-ups say “reserved GPU” prices. AWS limits the posted change to the Capacity Block families listed, and it says other Capacity Block prices, On-Demand, and Savings Plans are unchanged. The current tables still show more than one regional rate for some families, including P5 and P5en, while the October 7 notice states a single rate for each of those names. AWS does not say every current regional row rises by the same share.

results.title: AWS Capacity Blocks: ~15% GPU Hike Oct 7 | explainx.ai Blog | explainx.ai
results.author: Yash Thakker
highlights:
Effective October 7, 2026, Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML charge more for reserved NVIDIA accelerators. AWS published a single new hourly rate per family across all available regions: P6-B300 $16.146 ($16.819 GovCloud), P6-B200 $14.208 ($14.801 GovCloud), P5en $7.895, P5e $6.866, P5 $5.970, P4de $2.546, P4d $1.696. Compared with the tables still on that same page today, those US-listed NVIDIA families move about 15%.

This is a run-cost event, not a market-color event. If you already planned a reserved GPU block for a training run, a fine-tune window, or a burst of H100/H200/B200/B300 capacity, the invoice changes. On-Demand and Savings Plans do not move with this notice. The reservation fee is locked when you buy, even if the block starts after October 7. That is the mechanism. Use it or pay the new list.

Industry recaps this week have called the move a fourth consecutive quarterly hike on reserved GPU blocks. AWS's own page does not number the series. It says reservation prices are dynamic, update with supply and demand, and were already scheduled to update in October 2026. We cite the official rates below and compare them to the tables AWS still shows as current. We do not treat the "fourth quarter in a row" label as something Amazon itself wrote.

...

## The official October 7 rates (cite this page, not a recap)

AWS's announcement on the Capacity Blocks pricing page is the primary source. Quote it as written: reservation prices "are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand." Effective October 7, 2026, hourly rates per accelerator across all available AWS Regions will be the figures in the table below. "All other EC2 Capacity Block prices, as well as prices on fixed pricing models like On-Demand and Savings Plans, remain unchanged."

| Family | Accelerators (typical 8-way node) | New $ / accelerator-hour | GovCloud (if listed) | Today's table $ / accelerator (US examples) | Approx. delta vs today's US table |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | 8 × B300 on `p6-b300.48xlarge` | $16.146 | $16.819 | $14.04 | ~15% |
| P6-B200 | 8 × B200 on `p6-b200.48xlarge` | $14.208 | $14.801 | $12.355 | ~15% |
| P5en | 8 × H200 on `p5en.48xlarge` | $7.895 | — | $6.865 (US) | ~15% in US |
| P5e | 8 × H200 on `p5e.48xlarge` | $6.866 | — | $5.97 | ~15% |
| P5 | 8 × H100 on `p5.48xlarge` | $5.970 | — | $5.191 (US) | ~15% in US |
| P4de | 8 × A100 on `p4de.24xlarge` | $2.546 | — | $2.214 | ~15% |
| P4d | 8 × A100 on `p4d.24xlarge` | $1.696 | — | $1.475 | ~15% |

Instance-hour math is just eight times the accelerator-hour on the 48xlarge / 24xlarge shapes: a US `p5.48xlarge` that shows $41.528 today would be $47.76 at $5.970 × 8. A `p6-b300.48xlarge` that shows $112.32 today would be $129.168 at $16.146 × 8.

...

## What did not change (read this before you re-quote)

AWS split the SKU on purpose. Capacity Blocks are a reservation fee charged up front when you schedule the block, plus an operating-system fee while instances actually run. Linux OS on these shapes is $0.000 in the OS table; RHEL, SLES, and Ubuntu Pro still add their own hourly line. That OS table is not the October 7 NVIDIA hike.

Three other buckets stay on the old numbers unless AWS updates them separately:

1. On-Demand accelerated instances — different product, different price list.
2. Savings Plans — AWS grouped them with "fixed pricing models" that remain unchanged.
3. Capacity Block families not named in the October 7 sentence — today's page still lists P6e GB200 UltraServers (Dallas Local Zone, $10.582 per B200 on the u-p6e shapes) and Trn1 / Trn2 Trainium blocks. Those sit under "all other EC2 Capacity Block prices remain unchanged."

...

The lock sentence is the other operational detail: "Your Capacity Block is charged at the prevailing rate at the time of purchase, even if the Capacity Block is scheduled to start after the price is updated." Capacity Blocks can be reserved up to eight weeks ahead (AWS's product page). A November training window purchased on October 6 is still billed at today's table. The same window purchased on October 8 is billed at the new list. Start date is not the rate date.

...

The ~15% figure is not a slogan AWS printed. It is the ratio of the October 7 all-region list to the current per-accelerator numbers in the US rows of the same page. $16.146 / $14.04, $14.208 / $12.355, $5.970 / $5.191, $6.866 / $5.97, $7.895 / $6.865, $2.546 / $2.214, and $1.696 / $1.475 all land at about 1.15.

That ratio is not universal if your current row is already below the US table. AWS currently shows `p5.48xlarge` at $4.720 per H100 in several Asia Pacific, Europe, and South America regions versus $5.191 in US East/West. The October 7 sentence is a single P5 rate of $5.970 "across all available AWS Regions." $5.970 / $4.720 is about 26%, not 15%. `p5en.48xlarge` shows the same pattern: $6.865 in US rows versus $6.241 in several Europe and Asia Pacific rows, with a new all-region $7.895 (about 26% from $6.241).

...

- AWS can still edit the page. These numbers are as published on the Capacity Blocks pricing URL on October 1, 2026. If the banner or tables change before October 7, the banner wins.
- "Across all available AWS Regions" is AWS's wording. We flag the P5/P5en regional flattening as the important reading of that sentence. If AWS keeps regional discounts in the tables after October 7, use the tables.
- We do not have a first-party archive of every 2026 quarterly Capacity Blocks update, so we do not certify "fourth consecutive" or "first A100 hike of the year" as AWS claims.
- Perf/$ versus a new rack is out of scope. Rubin-class throughput stories do not reprice an H100 block you need in November.
- No customer-specific discounts. EDP, private pricing, and credits can dominate list. This post is list Capacity Blocks, not your contract.

...

Capacity Block list prices and the October 7, 2026 effective rates are accurate as of October 1, 2026 against AWS's public pricing page.

results.title: 15 GPU list prices rose in September and none fell. Today AWS raises Capacity Blocks 15% - DEV Community
results.author: FastGPU
highlights:
Today, October 7, AWS adds an increase of its own to EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML.

...

## AWS Capacity Blocks: 15% more from today, up to 26.5% outside the US 

AWS's Capacity Blocks pricing page says:

> Effective October 7, 2026, hourly rates per accelerator across all available AWS Regions will be: P6-B300 at $16.146 ($16.819 in AWS GovCloud Regions), P6-B200 at $14.208 ($14.801 in AWS GovCloud Regions), P5en at $7.895, P5e at $6.866, P5 at $5.970, P4de at $2.546, and P4d at $1.696.

Against the rates AWS published before, as recorded in our price-change log, per GPU per hour:

| Instance | GPU | Before | From Oct 7 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | B300 | $14.040 | $16.146 | +15.0% |
| P6-B200 | B200 | $12.355 | $14.208 | +15.0% |
| P5en, US Regions | H200 | $6.865 | $7.895 | +15.0% |
| P5en, Europe and Asia Pacific | H200 | $6.241 | $7.895 | +26.5% |
| P5e | H200 | $5.970 | $6.866 | +15.0% |
| P5, US Regions | H100 SXM | $5.191 | $5.970 | +15.0% |
| P5, Europe, Asia Pacific and South America | H100 SXM | $4.720 | $5.970 | +26.5% |
| P4de | A100 80GB | $2.214 | $2.546 | +15.0% |
| P4d | A100 40GB | $1.475 | $1.696 | +15.0% |

AWS now charges one rate in every Region, so blocks that used to be cheaper outside the US (P5 and P5en) rise the most. AWS publishes these rates to a tenth of a cent; our log shows them rounded to the cent. AWS also says Capacity Block reservation prices are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand, and: "All other EC2 Capacity Block prices, as well as prices on fixed pricing models like On-Demand and Savings Plans, remain unchanged."

## What it means if you rent 

- A Capacity Block is reserved capacity: you book a start date and a length, and AWS guarantees the GPUs for it. That is a different product from an on-demand GPU you can stop at any time. Still, for scale: the cheapest posted H100 SXM is $1.79/hr at Vast.ai as of 2026-10-07 01:46 UTC, the September-end median across 16 providers was $3.70/hr, and a P5 Capacity Block is now $5.970/hr.
- If you were planning a reserved block, re-run the numbers: the reserve-or-rent calculator has the October 7 rates, and the GPU cluster page prices N GPUs for M months across providers' published term rates.
- List prices change without notice. A price alert emails you when a GPU drops below a price you choose, with no account.

...

Posted prices, not transactions. The September report is computed from the recorded daily prices once the month is over and then frozen; every dated change is in the price-change log, also as JSON at `https://fastgpu.co/api/v1/price-changes`. The daily series is an open dataset (CC BY 4.0). Live prices in this post are as of 2026-10-07 01:46 UTC; the linked pages show the current ones. Some provider links on FastGPU are affiliate links; tables and every "cheapest" figure are ordered strictly by price.

...

Capacity Blocks for ML เป็นวิธีจองอินสแตนซ์ GPU ล่วงหน้าตามช่วงวันที่ต้องการ แทนการรอเครื่องว่างแบบ On-Demand หรือผูกสัญญาระยะยาว เอกสารของ AWS ระบุเงื่อนไขหลักไว้ดังนี้

results.title: You have until Tuesday to lock in today's H100 price on AWS. | Opsolute
results.author: Opsolute
highlights:
On Wednesday, October 7, AWS updates EC2 Capacity Block pricing. The headline number is a 15% increase. For H100s, that's only true in the US.

AWS is merging two regional price tiers into one global H100 (P5) rate:

• US regions: $5.191 → $5.970 per GPU-hour (+15%)
• Mumbai, Tokyo, Sydney, Jakarta, London, Stockholm, São Paulo: $4.720 → $5.970 per GPU-hour (+26.5%)

The cheaper regional tier is going away.

One detail makes this time-sensitive: a Capacity Block is billed at the rate in effect when you buy it, even if it starts weeks later. Buy before the change, and you lock in today's price.

If you reserve H100 capacity in any of those regions, check your plans now.
Only Capacity Block rates change. AWS says On-Demand and Savings Plans prices stay the same.

results.title: AWS Raised GPU Rental Prices Twice in 2026. Nebius Just Did It Again. — AIntOps
highlights:
AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block pricing for GPU instances roughly 15% in January 2026 and another 20% in July. Nebius raised its on-demand GPU prices again on October 1 — the second increase in three months, with some memory pricing up about 41%. Neither company frames these as one-time corrections. They read as a new baseline: the rental price of a GPU is no longer a number you can assume holds from one quarter to the next.

...

## AWS: two hikes, one product line

AWS's EC2 Capacity Block pricing for ML instances moved twice this year. The first increase, reported to take effect around January 4-6, raised rates on the P5 family by roughly 15% — p5e.48xlarge went from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour, and p5en.48xlarge from $36.18 to $41.61. Asked about the change, an AWS spokesperson told Data Center Dynamics it reflects "the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter." The second increase landed July 1, roughly 20%, across the P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de families — one report lists the P6-B300 now billing at $14.04 per accelerator-hour. Both changes applied specifically to Capacity Block reservations, not general on-demand EC2 pricing.

## What do AWS’s October GPU price changes reveal?

There is a timely pricing development alongside the financing report. AWS’s official EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing page announces increases for specified GPU reservations effective October 7, 2026. Selected published rates imply increases of approximately 15%.

| Capacity Blocks accelerator | Published rate before October 7 | Announced rate from October 7 | Approximate increase |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B300 in P6-B300 | $14.040 | $16.146 | 15% |
| B200 in P6-B200 | $12.355 | $14.208 | 15% |
| H100 in P5 | $5.191 | $5.970 | 15% |

Rates are in US dollars per accelerator-hour for the relevant non-GovCloud offerings. These are Capacity Blocks reservation prices. AWS states that other EC2 Capacity Blocks types, On-Demand prices and Savings Plans prices remain unchanged under this announcement.

Higher realized prices could improve returns on the affected capacity if customers continue booking it. However, the public rate card does not establish Amazon’s average realized GPU price, negotiated customer terms or the equipment mix in the proposed vehicle. Applying a 15% increase to all AWS revenue would be unjustified.

There is also a demand tradeoff.
